intro: We use I wish and if only to say that we would like reality to be different, now or in the past. They work like the conditionals: we move one tense back to show distance from reality.
objectifs: Express a wish about the present with wish / if only + past simple (or could).
Express regret about the past with wish / if only + past perfect.
Tell the difference between wish (unreal situation), hope (possible situation) and want.
Use if only for a stronger, more emotional wish.

sections.titre: Wishes about the present: wish + past simple
texte: For a present situation that we would like to be different, the verb after wish goes into the past simple. The past tense doesn't mean past time: it shows that this is not reality, as in the second conditional.
The pattern is: subject + wish + subject + past simple. That is possible but often left out (I wish that I had…).
With be, we use were with every subject in careful English (I wish I were, I wish it were). Was is common in speech.

lignes: I wish I had a car.
I would like to have one.
I live far from my family.
I wish I lived closer to my family.
I wish she weren't always late.

sections.titre: Wish + could: an ability you don't have
texte: To talk about an ability or possibility you don't have, use wish + could + base verb (could = past of can).
This is very common for languages, skills and blocked situations: “I wish I could stay longer.”
exemples: I wish I could speak Spanish.
I wish I could come to your wedding, but I'll be in Canada.
My son wishes he could drive.
He isn't able to drive yet.

sections.titre: Regrets about the past: wish + past perfect
texte: To regret something that happened (or didn't happen), put the verb in the past perfect (had + participle). It's the same step back as in the third conditional.
“I wish I hadn't said that” = I said it, and I'm sorry. We can also use regret + -ing (I regret saying that) or should have + participle (I should have listened).
exemples: I wish I had studied harder at school.
I didn't study hard; I regret it.
She wishes she hadn't sold her car.
She sold it; now she's sorry.
I wish I'd taken more photos in Kribi.

texte: If only means the same as I wish and uses the same tenses, but it is more emotional, often an exclamation: “If only I had more time!”
If only is often used alone, without a main clause, with an exclamation mark. It can also start a conditional sentence: “If only you had told me, I could have helped.”
exemples: If only I knew the answer!
If only we hadn't missed the train!

texte: Hope = a possible, realistic wish; it takes a normal tense (present or will): “I hope you pass your exam.” Wish = an unreal situation or one that can't be changed: “I wish I were younger.”
Want + to or want + someone + to: a simple desire (I want to leave, I want you to stay). We don't normally say “I wish you to…” in everyday English.

Wish + noun appears in fixed greetings: “I wish you a happy birthday”, “We wish you good luck”, “Best wishes”. To go further (wish + would to complain about someone's behaviour: “I wish you would stop”), see lesson 159.

lignes: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.
I wish I had brought an umbrella.
I wish you a merry Christmas.

formule: wish / if only + past simple (unreal present) · wish / if only + past perfect (past regret)
prononciation: wish /wɪʃ/: short i as in “it”, not /wiːʃ/. wishes /ˈwɪʃɪz/ has two syllables.
If only /ɪf ˈəʊnli/: stress on only, and often on the verb too: “If ONLY I'd LISTENED!”
In “I wish I'd known”, the 'd is very light but changes everything: without it, the sentence is about the present.
In “I wish I were”, were is weak /wə/: /aɪ ˈwɪʃ aɪ wə/.
A sigh or falling intonation often goes with regret: “I wish I could ↘.”
erreurs: I wish I have more time.
I wish I had more time.
A wish about the present: past simple after wish.
I wish I didn't say that yesterday.
I wish I hadn't said that yesterday.
A regret about the past: past perfect.
I wish you pass your exam.
I hope you pass your exam.
A possible wish: hope, not wish.
I wish I would be taller.
No would when talking about yourself: were / past simple.
I wish you to come to my party.
I'd like you to come to my party. / I hope you can come to my party.
Wish + someone + to is very formal and rare; use would like or hope.

dialogue.contexte: Montreal, in February. Kevin, who came from Libreville a year ago, talks to his colleague Julie outside the office.
lignes: It's minus twenty again. I wish it were summer!
You'll get used to it. Do you miss Gabon?
Get used to = become familiar with.
A lot. I wish my parents lived closer. I can't visit them often.
I hope you can go back this summer.
Me too. And I wish I'd bought a warmer coat before the winter!
If only you'd asked me! I know a great shop.
Really? I wish I could go there now.
Come on, it's open until nine. Let's go!

exercices.consigne: Say if the sentence is a wish about the present (P) or a regret about the past (R).
items: I wish I had a bigger flat.
P
I wish I had listened to my teacher.
R
If only she were here!
P
He wishes he hadn't moved to the city.
R

exercices.consigne: Complete with the correct form of the verb for a wish about the present.
items: I don't have a car. I wish I ___ a car.
had
I can't swim. I wish I ___ swim.
could
My flat is very small. I wish it ___ bigger.
were (was)
We live in a noisy street. I wish we ___ in a quiet street.
lived
He doesn't speak English. He wishes he ___ English.
spoke (could speak)

exercices.consigne: Complete to express a regret about the past.
items: I didn't go to the concert. I wish I ___ to the concert.
had gone
She said something rude. She wishes she ___ it.
hadn't said
We didn't take any photos. If only we ___ some photos!
had taken
I ate too much cake. I wish I ___ so much.
hadn't eaten

exercices.consigne: Choose wish or hope, in the correct form.
items: I ___ you have a good trip to Dakar.
hope
I ___ I were on holiday right now.
wish
We ___ the weather will be nice tomorrow.
hope
She ___ she had studied medicine.
wishes

exercices.titre: 5. Rewrite with wish or if only
exercices.consigne: Rewrite each sentence with the words in brackets.
items: I can't play the guitar. (I wish)
I wish I could play the guitar.
I didn't call her, and I'm sorry. (I wish)
I wish I had called her.
It's raining, and I hate it. (If only)
If only it wasn't (weren't) raining!
She left her job, and now she regrets it. (She wishes)
She wishes she hadn't left her job.

exercices.consigne: Write 4 true sentences: two wishes about your life now (wish + past simple / could) and two regrets about your past (wish / if only + past perfect).
items: Example answer
I wish I had more time to read. I wish I could speak Dutch, because many of my colleagues in Brussels speak it. I wish I had started learning English earlier. If only I hadn't sold my old guitar!

a_retenir: Unreal present: wish / if only + past simple (I wish I had…, I wish it were…).
An ability you don't have: wish + could (I wish I could swim).
Past regret: wish / if only + past perfect (I wish I had listened).
A possible, realistic wish: hope + present / will, not wish.
If only = wish, but stronger and more emotional.
